Replay

P2P timing and benchmark contract

3 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Measurements

Use P2P profiling to measure step, replay, checksum and pump costs, and the delay between local input capture and simulation. Profiling is optional runtime state. It is excluded from the match contract, canonical state, archives and checksums. Enable it with a monotonic microsecond clock after creating or restoring the Runner:

Odin
p2p.profile_set(&peer, replay.Profile_Clock{user = clock_data, read = clock_read})
samples := peer.profile.metrics[.Replay]
p95_upper_us := replay.timing_percentile_upper(samples, 95)

profile_set resets metrics and pending capture marks. Use it whenever changing clock domains; assigning a new clock directly could combine incompatible timestamps. Passing an empty clock disables collection and frees capture-mark storage. Destroy frees it as part of the Runner. A failed/backward clock records diagnostic errors without changing gameplay or network policy. Disabled collection has no clock calls or capture allocation. The remaining branches are still part of runner execution.

Metric Measured interval
Step One attempted forward Timeline.advance, including state/input validation and commit
Replay One attempted suffix revision, including prediction rewriting and staged simulation
Hash One confirmed canonical state/event chain update
Pump Protocol polling/decoding, repair, confirmation, retransmission and timeout work
Input_Latency Local input capture to the end of the first successful forward step that uses it

Step/Replay/Hash/Pump are operation wall times, not CPU accounting. Pump contains some replay/hash intervals, so their totals must not be added together. They exclude Godot rendering, normal event-journal processing and game UI; the clock itself adds measurement overhead. Histogram percentiles are conservative bounds. The final overflow bucket uses the maximum observed duration. Zero samples return zero.

Input latency is separate from work time. A configured delay of D at hz gives D/hz seconds of nominal scheduling delay; waiting at the prediction horizon and frame catch-up change elapsed time. The metric covers the captured value, including held/neutral inputs, and records it once on first application. It does not measure device polling delay, an engine render submission, physical display latency or final confirmation. A restored future input has no valid timestamp from the new process, so it contributes no latency sample. Samples begin with newly captured inputs. stats.max_replay_depth records the maximum completed successful revision depth. The authoritative runner's net.Profile_Clock aliases the same clock type, so one provider can instrument both runner styles. Keep borrowed clock user data alive until profiling is disabled or the runtime is destroyed.

Measurements#

Shell
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_p2p/bench.sh
REPLAY_KEEP_LOGS=1 nix develop --command bash examples/replay_duel/profile_run.sh

The native benchmark executes two complete peers plus deterministic Memory transport for 2,400 ticks. LAN and faulted two/eight-delay cases use the same inputs, including eight initial neutral ticks, and must produce the same whole reference world and event chain. The fault clock is accelerated: seven latency ticks, two jitter ticks, 10% loss and 10% duplication. CPU is measured with getrusage(SELF) user+system time; wall time uses a monotonic clock. Setup, reference construction/comparison and cleanup are excluded. Memory transport and codec work are included. These totals are not per-peer CPU or Godot CPU measurements.

Five measured trials follow a warm-up per case, alternating profiling on/off order. The report uses medians and verifies identical protocol work with profiling enabled. Its operation histograms describe the optimized native build. Input-latency samples are intentionally omitted from this accelerated-loop report because they would describe execution speed, not real-time network delay. The benchmark is a standalone measurement tool; it imposes no machine-dependent performance threshold.

The Godot comparison runs actual ENet processes with 120 ms receive delay per side, 0–20 ms jitter, 10% loss and 10% duplication. It compares two/eight input-delay ticks, an eight-tick prediction limit and the same 600-tick input sequence (eight initial neutral ticks). Both configurations verify the same whole world; each reports capture-to-simulation latency, work timing, replay depth, waiting attempts, elapsed time and dropped render-clock accumulation. Results are individual-run observations, not a hardware-independent responsiveness guarantee or a Kit-versus-Replay comparison.

Set RDP_PROFILE=1 on other Duel runs to collect timings. RDP_DELAY and RDP_PREDICTION select the fixed protocol configuration; all participants must agree. RDP_NEUTRAL controls only the automated fixture's initial neutral-input prefix.
